newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. agency chief says budget cuts mean slow death.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency chief says budget cuts mean slow death.

text.p: The head of the U.N. environment agency defended her record on Wednesday against critics led by the United States and told governments they were condemning UNEP to a slow death by under-funding.

In a vigorous counter-attack, Elizabeth Dowdeswell announced publicly for the first time she would not seek to extend her mandate as executive director of the Nairobi-based United Nations Environment Programme.

Dowdeswell, a Canadian, told ministers and senior delegates from many of UNEP's 185 member states that the agency's problems were chiefly due to constant budget cuts and lack of political support, rather than bad management.

"...this governing council is your last opportunity to save this organisation. Neither you nor I want UNEP to slip into irrelevance. But if you do not equip it and empower it to succeed, it can only fail, silently," Dowdeswell said.

Her speech at the opening of the UNEP governing council's ministerial session ended with a standing ovation by about half the delegates, reflecting the split views on her stewardship and the role of the global U.N. agency.
"It was a very strong speech and by confirming that she is leaving Dowdeswell may force UNEP's critics to be more generous on the budget," one Asian delegate told Reuters.
The U.S. delegation said last week UNEP was disjointed and in a state of crisis.
"Throwing more money at UNEP's problems is not an answer to the problems," U.S. delegate William Dilday said, voicing arguments his government is using for a total overhaul of the U.N. system.
The new U.S.-backed secretary-general of the United Nations, Kofi Annan, has pledged to make reforms but also wants the United States to settle its debts of about $1 billion.
For the ministerial session ending on Friday, which will decide on UNEP funding for next year, Washington has sent Assistant secretary of state Eileen Claussen to Nairobi.
UNEP's budget has declined from $160 million in 1991-92 to $105 million during the last two years.
Dowdeswell, whose first term was previously extended by only one year to the end of 1997, said more cuts would be fatal.
"Surgery alone cannot succeed as the cure for this starving patient. It must be remembered that UNEP's budgets are overall vastly insufficient," she said.

Kenya's vice-president, George Saitoti, told the opening session his country was honoured to host UNEP and wanted the agency turned into a "Global Environmental Authority" with a broader and clearer mandate.
The best-received speech was by Maurice Njoroge, a Kenyan speaking for the world's youth who was chosen because, like UNEP, he is 25 years old.
Njoroge, unperturbed by the presence of the vice-president, told delegates about the miserable environment in which most people in the world live.
He compared the spotless and luxurious U.N. compound at Gigiri with the huge slum of Mathere where he lives.
"Although we live just down the road, we have none of the things you have here. We lack clean water, roads, electricity, toilets, garbage collection facilities, health and security," he said.
